1310.title: The three gunas on your plate
1310.hook: Arjuna asks Krishna about faith, and the answer arrives as three kinds of food
1310.carry: the three gunas show up on your plate
1310.tomorrow: Let the guest be a god
1310.howItsDone: Hindus who draw on the Bhagavad Gita speak of food as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, after the three gunas in its chapter seventeen; many families keep a sattvic kitchen on holy days and fasts, some avoiding onion and garlic, and offer food before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Ashvapati's lesson: eating is an offering to God, the fire within, taken unhurried, with the mind on the food.

On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, deep into the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna a sharp question. What about people who worship with real faith, but set aside the rules in the books? Where do they stand? Krishna's answer goes somewhere unexpected. Faith comes in three kinds, he says, and a person is made of their faith: as someone's faith is, so they are. Then, to show how deep that runs, he turns to something everyone does every day. Even the food people love, he says, comes in three kinds.
screen: `WHAT ABOUT FAITH WITHOUT THE RULES?` → `A PERSON IS MADE OF THEIR FAITH.` → `EVEN FOOD COMES IN THREE KINDS.`

segments.voice: The three kinds follow the three gunas, one of Hinduism's big ideas: three qualities running through all of nature, and through every person. Sattva, clarity. Rajas, restlessness. Tamas, heaviness. Sattvic food, paraphrased, increases life, vigor, strength, health, happiness and contentment: savory, smooth, nourishing, pleasing to the heart. Rajasic food is too bitter, too sour, too salty, too hot, too sharp, too dry, burning, and the verse says it brings pain, grief and sickness. Tamasic food is stale, tasteless, gone off, left over, unclean. Notice how Krishna sorts them: by effects. Sattvic food is defined by what it gives, rajasic food by what it leaves behind. The test is the hour after. And the second list is full of too: hot and sour aren't banned, it's the excess that tips a meal into restlessness. Now put it beside Arjuna's question. A person is made of their faith, and the food a person loves comes in the same three kinds. So the plate isn't separate from the spiritual life; it's part of it. Every meal leans a little toward clarity, restlessness or heaviness, and so does the one eating it. That's why many Hindu families keep a sattvic kitchen on holy days and fasts: simple, fresh food, and in many homes no onion or garlic, a custom drawn from later teaching rather than from these verses. And it turns the question around. Not only, what should I eat. Also, what does what I reach for say about who I'm becoming?
screen: `THE THREE GUNAS: CLARITY, RESTLESSNESS, HEAVINESS` · `LIFE, STRENGTH, HEALTH, JOY` · `TOO HOT, TOO SHARP, PAIN AFTER` · `A SATTVIC KITCHEN ON HOLY DAYS`

segments.voice: Bring to mind what you ate most recently, and the hour after it: light and clear, restless and a little wired, or heavy and dull. No score; just notice which guna it leaned toward. Then picture your next plate, and before the first bite, offer it first, the way many Hindu families do, with a short prayer or a silent thanks. If you don't pray, simply look at the food for one full breath before you eat.
Food as practice. The Gita's three kinds of food, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, following the three gunas, sorted by what they do to the eater. Today's word.
Your line: the three gunas show up on your plate. Krishna's test is the hour after. See you tomorrow.

1311.title: Let the guest be a god
1311.hook: a knock at the door just as dinner is served: the Upanishad says to make much food for exactly this
1311.carry: let the guest be a god to you
1311.howItsDone: Hindu teaching treats feeding a guest as sacred, in the Upanishad's words, let the guest be a god to you; in some Hindu homes a first portion of the meal is set aside for a guest, a cow or birds before the family eats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three gunas on the plate: food sorted by what it does to the eater, and the hour after.

Dinner is on the table, exactly enough for the people sitting at it, counted out, served. And then a knock at the door. A cousin passing through, a neighbor, a friend of a friend who's hungry and a little embarrassed about the timing. Everyone at the table does the same quick arithmetic. The Taittiriya Upanishad, the same text where Bhrigu found food, has already thought about this knock, and its answer comes before the knock does. Today, food that doesn't stop at your own plate.
screen: `DINNER, COUNTED OUT.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `THE ANSWER COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Near the end of Bhrigu's story, the Upanishad gives this rule, paraphrased: do not turn away anyone who comes to your dwelling for shelter. And so, it says, gather much food, so there is food to give. That's the answer to the knock. Not a quick calculation at the door, but a kitchen that cooks, from the start, for more than the people already sitting down. Earlier, in its teaching to departing students, the same Upanishad says, in Sanskrit, atithi devo bhava: let the guest be a god to you. The guest isn't a disruption to the meal; the guest is honored at it like a god. The Bhagavad Gita says it from the other side. Krishna says, paraphrased, that good people who eat what remains after the offering are freed from their faults, but those who cook only for their own sake eat their own wrong. This lands in three places. First, this is why a Hindu home feeds a visitor before asking anything else: the guest is honored as God arriving at the door. Food as practice is also food as hospitality. Second, the order matters: offer first, eat what remains. In some Hindu homes a first portion is set aside before the family eats, for a guest, for a cow, for the birds. Third, it's practical. Make a little more. Keep a spare plate. The rule isn't a feeling about generosity; it's a way of cooking, decided before anyone knocks.

segments.voice: Picture the place where you usually eat, add one more seat, and let a face come for it: a friend you haven't fed in a while, a neighbor, someone alone. Hold that face kindly with the breath, or if no one comes, hold the empty seat itself, open. If you pray, hold that person in prayer.
Food as practice. In the Upanishad: turn no one away, and make much food; let the guest be a god to you. Food that doesn't stop at your own plate. Today's word.
Your line: let the guest be a god to you. A kitchen that cooks for one more is ready for the knock. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1312.title: Shvetaketu and the ember
1312.hook: a proud student is told to stop eating, and his father's lesson arrives as an ember
1312.carry: the mind is made of food
1312.howItsDone: Some Hindus fast on particular days as a devotional practice, while teachers of the Upanishads read Uddalaka's experiment as a lesson about the self, not as a fasting rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, let the guest be a god to you: make much food, and turn no one away.

A student comes home after years of study, sure of himself, full of verses. You met him back in year three, the proud one: Shvetaketu. His father, Uddalaka, decides to test him, and the test isn't a debate. It's a diet. Eat nothing for a while, the father says. Drink all the water you like. Then come back and recite what you know. The experiment sits in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. Today, what a meal has to do with a mind.
screen: `A STUDENT HOME, SURE OF HIMSELF.` → `THE TEST IS A DIET.` → `WHAT A MEAL HAS TO DO WITH A MIND.`

segments.voice: It starts with a claim, paraphrased. Food, once eaten, divides three ways. The coarsest part leaves the body. The middle part becomes flesh. The finest part becomes mind. Uddalaka puts it in one line, in Sanskrit annamayam hi somya manah: the mind, my dear, is made of food. Water, he adds, becomes breath, and heat becomes speech. Then the test. The text says fifteen days without food, with water allowed. Shvetaketu comes back, and his father asks for the verses. They don't come to me, sir, he says. So Uddalaka gives him a picture. A great fire has burned down to one ember, the size of a firefly. It can't burn much now. Add straw, and it blazes again. Go and eat. Shvetaketu eats, comes back, and the verses are all there. And he understood, the text says. Three things. First, it's humbling. The young scholar who thought learning lived somewhere above the body finds it leaning on lunch. Second, it's kind to the body. Nobody is scolded for needing to eat; the plate is part of how a person thinks. Third, it's a doorway. In this same chapter Uddalaka will say tat tvam asi, you are that: the self, atman, is one with the reality in everything. He's leading his son there, and food is one of the first things he reaches for. And plainly, since these days hold Ayurveda to a careful standard: this is a teaching story, not a fasting plan, and nobody should copy the experiment. What it offers is a way to see a meal: not fuel poured in while the real you is somewhere else, but an ember being fed.
screen: `FOOD DIVIDES THREE WAYS` · `THE MIND, MY DEAR, IS MADE OF FOOD` · `AN EMBER THE SIZE OF A FIREFLY` · `A TEACHING STORY, NOT A FASTING PLAN`

segments.voice: Rest a hand low on the belly if you like, and let a small ember come to mind, glowing, about the size of a firefly. With each breath in let it brighten a little, the way a coal brightens when air reaches it, and with each breath out let it settle and glow. If you pray, give thanks for the food that is holding you up right now.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya, the finest part of a meal becomes mind, and a hungry student's verses come back after he eats. Today's word.
Your line: the mind is made of food. Feed the ember, the way Uddalaka sent his son to eat. Rest well.

1313.title: Narada and the far shore
1313.hook: a sage who has read everything is still in sorrow, and the last step across is what he takes in
1313.carry: everything you take in feeds the mind
1313.howItsDone: Some Hindus cite the Chandogya's line aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih to explain care about what and how they eat, and Vedanta teachers following Shankara apply it to everything a person takes in through the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uddalaka's ember, and let the guest be a god to you at its root: the mind is made of food.

The sage Narada comes to the teacher Sanatkumara with a long list. The four Vedas, the old stories, grammar, mathematics, the stars, the arts. I've learned all of it, he says, and I'm still in sorrow. I know words, not the self, and I've heard that the one who knows the self crosses over sorrow. Take me across. The seventh chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad is the long road across. And at the very end, the last step it gives Narada isn't another book. It's what he takes in.
screen: `I'VE LEARNED IT ALL.` → `AND I'M STILL IN SORROW.` → `TAKE ME ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the chain, paraphrased. When what is taken in is pure, the inner being is pure. When the inner being is pure, memory becomes steady. When memory is steady, all the knots are loosened. In Sanskrit it begins aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih. Ahara is what's taken in. Sattva is the inner being, the mind at its clearest. And the text adds: to Narada, his stains wiped away, Sanatkumara showed the far shore beyond darkness. Notice three things. First, the direction. It runs from the plate inward, from something as plain as a meal to the very thing Narada came for: crossing over sorrow. Second, memory here isn't remembering where the keys are. Readers in the Vedanta tradition take it as a steady remembering of who one really is: the self, atman, the thing Narada admitted he didn't know. Third, the knots. The text doesn't name them. Readers have heard in them the tangles that bind a person: craving, confusion, old fears. Then the scholar's turn. Shankara, the great Vedanta teacher, reads ahara more widely than food: everything gathered in by the senses, what the eyes take in, what the ears take in. Pure intake, not just a pure plate. This is ahara shuddhi, purity of what's taken in. It's why many Hindus take care over what they eat and offer it first, and why many teachers apply the same care to what a person watches and listens to. Narada had filled himself with words and stayed in sorrow. The chain says: watch what you take in, and the way across gets clearer.
screen: `PURE INTAKE, PURE INNER BEING` · `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED` · `AHARA: ALL THAT'S TAKEN IN` · `THE FAR SHORE BEYOND DARKNESS`

segments.voice: Go back through the day so far, not only meals: what the eyes took in, a screen, a street, a face, and what the ears took in, voices, music, news, letting each pass without grading it. Then find one knot somewhere, a tightness something left behind, and with each breath out let it loosen a little, if it will. If you pray, hold that knot in prayer.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya's chain, pure intake, a clear inner being, steady memory, and every knot loosened. Today's word.
Your line: everything you take in feeds the mind. Ahara, not just the plate. See you tomorrow.

1314.title: Kumbhakarna's long sleep
1314.hook: a giant opens his mouth to ask for power, and asks for sleep
1314.carry: yoga is for the one who sleeps in measure
1314.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavad Gita treat measured sleep and waking as part of yoga, and Ayurveda's classical routine counts sleep at the right hour among the three supports of life; Kumbhakarna is the household name for anyone who oversleeps.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Narada and the far shore: everything you take in feeds the mind.

Three brothers sit in fierce penance for thousands of years, and the creator Brahma comes to grant each a wish. The gods are terrified of the middle brother. Kumbhakarna is a giant with an appetite to match, and they fear what he'll ask for. So, in the Ramayana's telling, Brahma calls on Sarasvati, goddess of speech, and she slips onto Kumbhakarna's tongue. He opens his mouth to ask for his boon, and what comes out is: let me sleep. For years.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS, THREE BOONS.` → `SARASVATI ON HIS TONGUE.` → `LET ME SLEEP.`

segments.voice: He gets his wish, and the giant who could have shaken the heavens spends his life asleep. In the popular telling he sleeps six months at a time and wakes for a single day. When Rama's army reaches Lanka, his brother Ravana needs him, and waking him takes drums, conches, mountains of food and elephants marched over his body. He wakes, he fights bravely, and he falls. Plenty of Indian families still tease a child who won't get out of bed: get up, Kumbhakarna. Behind the joke is a real teaching. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, paraphrased: yoga isn't for one who eats too much or not at all, nor for one who sleeps too much or stays awake too long. For the one measured in food and play, in work, in sleep and waking, yoga ends sorrow. Elsewhere he names tamas, the heavy guna, as binding a person through carelessness, laziness and sleep. So the Hindu teaching isn't that sleep is good or bad. It's measure. Ayurveda says it from the doctor's side. The Charaka Samhita names three supports, upastambha, that keep a life standing: food, sleep, and brahmacharya, a disciplined way of living. Happiness and strength, knowing and not knowing, it says, depend on sleep taken rightly or wrongly, in the right measure and at the right time. So there are two ways to miss: Kumbhakarna's lost years, and the all-nighter. For anyone trading sleep for deadlines, that's the teaching: the night is part of the practice, not time stolen from it. Sleep trouble that lasts, or exhaustion that won't lift, goes to a doctor.

1315.title: Sleep as going home
1315.hook: a bird tied to a peg flies every direction, then lands where it's tied
1315.carry: in sleep, the self goes home to being
1315.howItsDone: Some Vedanta teachers read Uddalaka's lesson on sleep as a hint about the self, and the tethered bird is used in teaching to show the mind coming to rest in the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kumbhakarna slept his strength away, and Krishna asked for yoga is for the one who sleeps in measure in measure.
screen: `YOGA IS FOR THE ONE WHO SLEEPS IN MEASURE IN MEASURE.`

segments.voice: A bird is tied to a peg by a long string. It takes off toward the trees, and the string pulls it up short. It tries the other way, toward the roof. Short again. It tries every direction there is. Finally, worn out, it comes down and settles right at the peg, the one place it was tied all along. That picture comes from Uddalaka, the father who taught his son with an ember. In the very next part of the Chandogya Upanishad, he turns to his son and says: learn from me about sleep.
screen: `A BIRD ON A STRING.` → `EVERY DIRECTION, PULLED SHORT.` → `IT SETTLES AT THE PEG.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka starts with a word. The Sanskrit for he sleeps is svapiti, and the text plays on it: svam apita, gone to his own. When a person sleeps, he says, paraphrased, he has gone home, united with sat, the Existent, being itself. That's why people say he sleeps: he has gone to his own. It's the Upanishad's own wordplay, a teacher's hook, not a dictionary entry. But look at what it does to the night. Sleep stops being a switch-off and becomes a homecoming. Then the bird. Tied to a peg, it flies in every direction, finds no resting place anywhere else, and settles where it's tied. In the same way, Uddalaka says, the mind flies in every direction, finds no resting place elsewhere, and settles down in the breath. For the mind, my dear, is tied to the breath. Three things in the picture. First, the day as flight. Messages, errands, worries, plans: the mind goes out and out, and it's meant to. The bird isn't scolded for flying. Second, the tether isn't a cage. It's what makes landing possible; without the peg, there'd be nowhere to come down. Third, the tether is close. Not a mountain, not a far temple. The breath, going the whole time under all the flying. This is the Upanishads' great teaching in small: your deepest self, atman, is one with sat, being itself, what other Upanishads call Brahman. A few lines on, Uddalaka sums it up for his son: tat tvam asi, you are that. Every night, in his teaching, everyone takes the trip home, whether they notice or not.
screen: `SVAPITI: GONE TO HIS OWN` · `SLEEP AS A HOMECOMING` · `THE BIRD SETTLES AT ITS TETHER` · `THE MIND IS TIED TO THE BREATH`

segments.voice: Let the mind go wherever it likes for a while, tomorrow, yesterday, a conversation, a list, without chasing it back. 1316.title: The dreamer is self-lit
1316.hook: a king keeps asking what a person's light is, after the sun, the moon and the fire are gone
1316.carry: the self is its own light
1316.tomorrow: What's left when even the dreams stop?
1316.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers read Yajnavalkya's teaching on the dream as a pointer to the self as the light of awareness, and study the waking, dreaming and deep-sleep states together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga is for the one who in sleep, the self goes home to beings in measure as going home: the mind settling in the breath like a bird at its peg.

What light does a person have? King Janaka puts that to the sage Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and the answers come one at a time. The sun, Yajnavalkya says: by its light a person sits, goes out, works and comes home. And when the sun has set? The moon. And when the moon has set too? Fire. And when the fire goes out? Speech: in the dark, a person goes toward a voice. And when speech goes quiet as well? Then, Yajnavalkya says, the self is his light. Today, the dream.
screen: `WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON HAVE?` → `SUN, MOON, FIRE, SPEECH.` → `AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?`

segments.voice: Why go there? Because Yajnavalkya is about to talk about dreaming, and dreaming is the proof. At night there's no sun, no lamp, no voice. And yet a whole world shows up: streets, faces, a house you've never lived in that is somehow your house. What's lighting it? The text's answer, paraphrased: in the dream, the person becomes his own light. The Sanskrit is svayam jyotih, self-lit. Then a passage worth hearing slowly. There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads, but he makes chariots, horses and roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, but he makes joys and pleasures. There are no ponds, no lotus pools, no rivers, but he makes ponds, lotus pools and rivers. For he is a maker. What is the passage after? First, the dream as evidence. Yajnavalkya isn't interested in what a dream means; this isn't a dream dictionary. He points at the fact that dreams happen at all, that something keeps seeing when every outer light is off. Second, the dreamer as maker. Every road in the dream was built that night, by the one asleep. Third, the turn back to waking. If something in a person can light a whole world in the dark, the same light is there at noon, quietly doing the seeing behind the eyes. That's where Yajnavalkya is steering his king: the self, atman, isn't one more thing you see. It's the light you see by. And one honest note: this is the Upanishad's teaching about the self, not a claim about how the brain dreams. It asks you to notice something, not to accept a theory.
screen: `NO SUN, NO LAMP, AND YET A WORLD` · `SVAYAM JYOTIH: SELF-LIT` · `NO CHARIOTS, BUT HE MAKES THEM` · `THE SAME LIGHT AT NOON`

segments.voice: Close the eyes and let whatever appears come and go, a color, a face, a room from this morning, without following any of it. Then turn gently toward whatever is seeing them; don't try to find it, just rest in the fact that the seeing hasn't stopped. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
